lignes.texte: Somewhere in your living room there’s a 65-inch rectangle that’s spying on you.
Every single second, your television is tracking everything you watch. Every show,
every movie, every game you play. What was supposed to be entertainment has turned
into a digital wiretap, harvesting your data every moment of the day.
They told you they were doing this… but they buried it in 80 pages of fine print.
Now, state prosecutors have had enough. Texas has launched a massive legal war over this.
They allege major manufacturers are taking screenshots of your tv every 500 milliseconds.
Big Brother is watching you… and they’re selling off your private data to the highest bidder.
Anytime you switch on a tv and settle, you might think it’s just you and the screen.
It’s not.
According to lawsuits filed by the State of Texas, every half second, your television is analyzing
whatever’s on the screen. It doesn’t save a full recording. Instead, it takes a tiny sample,
a few pixels here and a snippet of audio there. The tv instantly converts them into
a unique digital “fingerprint,” and fires it off to a remote server. You’ll never get to see it.
But it’s matched against a global database, where all your viewing habits are catalogued.
What show, what season, what episode and the night you watched it.
It’s called Automated Content Recognition, or ACR.
And the lawsuits allege, the software was switched the moment you took your TV out of its box.
ACR works at the level of the screen, so it isn’t contingent on what streaming platform you’re
paying for. Use a cable box? Fingerprinted. PlayStation? Fingerprinted. That dusty DVD
of your wedding plugged in through an HDMI? According to the complaints, that’s fair game,
too. Anything that makes it onto the glass is potentially something it reports on.
That’s precisely what set Texas off.
In December 2025, Attorney General Ken Paxton sued 5 of the biggest television makers on Earth in
one sweep. Samsung, LG, Sony, Hisense, and TCL were all in his crosshairs. His office called
the whole setup “a mass surveillance system” sitting in millions of American living rooms.
Within days, a judge had issued a temporary restraining order
against Hisense. Samsung got one in January 2026. Just one month later,
Samsung had settled and agreed to stop collecting ACR data from Texans without
their explicit consent. LG followed in May. The other 3 are still fighting their corner.
The penalties in play aren’t pocket change. Texas's consumer protection law allows up
to $10,000 per violation. This is the same office that squeezed $1.4 billion out of Meta.
Multiply "per violation" by every smart TV in a state of
31 million people and you'll see why TV makers' lawyers started panicking.
IThe most damning independent investigation of
all didn't use a bargain-bin smart TV set from a WalMart. It used an LG G5,
one of the priciest OLEDs the company makes. Paying more doesn't buy you privacy, it turns out.
It just buys sharper surveillance.
LG alone has sold an estimated 216 million smart TVs worldwide. That's more screens than there
are people in Brazil, and that's before you count Samsung, Sony, and the others.
How did the humble television turn into a source of corporate espionage?
The answer lies with a company that got caught, paid a fine of about 20 cents per TV and a slap
on the wrist. And that taught the entire industry a multi-billion dollar lesson.
Spying is cheap… if you do it right.
Walk through a Best Buy or Wal-Mart and you’ll see a wall of suspiciously
affordable 55-inch TVs. Most of them are made by a company called Vizio.
Starting in 2014, according to the FTC, these TVs were recording what their owners watched second
by second. The feature had a friendly, innocuous name. “Smart Interactivity.” The FTC revealed that
the TVs described this as nothing more than a tool for “program offers and suggestions.” It didn’t
mention the part where you’re viewing history got packaged up and sold to the highest bidder.
It wasn’t just new TVs either.
Vizio used a software update to force the tracking onto older sets that people already
owned. Consumers went to bed with a regular TV and woke up with an informant in their bedroom.
Vizio boasted that the system was hoovering up as
many as 100 billion data points a day from millions of screens. That data,
the FTC said, was sold to third parties and paired with details from data brokers.
The level of detail got pretty granular.
It didn’t just know that someone in Ohio was watching Jeopardy. By matching IP addresses
with external databases, it could figure out that specific viewer was a married,
college-educated homeowner in their 40s watching Jeopardy! followed by 3 hours of Forged in Fire.
In February 2017, the FTC and the State of New Jersey caught up with them. The
case covered 11 million TVs, and Vizio settled for $2.2 million.
The settlement worked out at less than a gumball per TV. Vizio also paid $17 million to settle a
separate class action. It sounds bigger until you understand how much that data was worth.
Each person whose data was taken was entitled to a $17 to $31 share of the
settlement. For 3 years of a machine in your house watching you watch it.
Vizio wasn’t even the first to get caught.
In 2013, Jason Huntley, an IT consultant from England, started to suspect his new
LG television was up to something nefarious. So, he started monitoring its network traffic.
He discovered the TV was phoning home to LG every time he changed the channel. He dug
into the settings and found an option to turn off the collection of watching info.
So, he switched it off.
And the TV kept doing it anyway.
Then things got really weird. Huntley plugged a USB stick into the TV and
uncovered a digital horror show. The TV was scanning the drive and sending
the names of the files back to LG’s servers in unencrypted plain text. Private holiday videos,
kids’ birthday parties and embarrassing filenames, the TV was reading the labels and snitching.
When he complained, LG's customer support reportedly told him he'd agreed to the terms
and conditions when he bought the TV. If Huntley had a problem, he could take it up with the store.
Meanwhile, LG’s own marketing was promising advertisers that their “LG Smart Ad analyses
users' favourite programs, online behavior, search keywords and other information.”
After the story blew up, LG pulled the promo video and promised a software fix.
So by 2017, the industry had 2 lessons in front of it. First,
people hate being spied on. Second, when you get caught, the bill is tiny.
Guess which lesson stuck?
By 2026, most people had made their peace with the idea that their TV knew
what they watched. Then a YouTube channel decided to find out what else it knew.
Gamers Nexus, a hardware channel better known for tearing apart graphics cards,
teamed up with Wendell Wilson of Level1Techs and a few independent security researchers.
They spent more than 500 hours and roughly $70,000 taking apart retail LG OLED TVs,
including one of the most expensive sets LG sells.
They hooked the TVs up to network-monitoring software and watched what went in and out,
like a stakeout, except the suspect was bolted to their living room wall.
The first thing they caught was the TV counting devices.
The TV was sweeping the home network and identifying everything connected to it:
phones, PCs, printers, network switches, smart-home gadgets.
LG denied the spying claims but confirmed its TVs scan for nearby devices and called it “a
standard function of all smart TVs and other smart home devices.” Which it is.
And that's the problem.
Next, the investigation found ACR still fingerprinting the screen while the TV was
being used as a plain monitor over HDMI. So plugging in a gaming PC or a Blu-ray
player doesn’t route around the snooping. It just feeds the prying eyes more material.
Then came the microphones.
The team reported that the TV's microphone stayed live for 10 to
15 seconds after someone stopped speaking. Long enough to catch the end of “Hi LG,
play Bluey” and the beginning of whatever you said to your spouse afterwards.
The most unnerving demonstration came with an asterisk…
And it’s an important one.
Researchers showed that a compromised LG TV could record audio while it appeared
to be switched off. It could store it while disconnected from the internet,
and then send it to servers once the connection came back.
Sure, they had to break into the TV first to uncover all of this. But that’s not
exactly comforting when you learn they also found remote-code-execution vulnerabilities,
the kind of holes that could let a stranger do that breaking-in over
the network. The details are being withheld while LG patches them.
LG’s official verdict on the whole thing was that the claims were obviously not true. The company
says it only processes voices when the mic button is pressed or the wake word is uttered. They want
consumers to believe that the microphones are completely silent until they’re activated.
But LG openly bragged about the size of their surveillance network:
216 million smart TVs. The number wasn’t a secret. It was right there in the
sales brochure sent out by the company’s advertising division to secure ad revenue.
Companies keep getting away with this. Why?
Because you gave them explicit permission. You just don’t remember.
Every tech company in this story employs the same defense. That you consented when
you bought their TV. Technically, that’s true. Somewhere in the 15 minutes between unboxing
your TV and watching your first show, a screen appeared and you pressed a button.
That button meant yes.
Let’s talk about what you agreed to.
Start with the paperwork. Smart TV privacy policies run to tens
of thousands of words across multiple linked documents. On some sets they're
displayed on screen about 5 lines at a time, scrolled with a remote control.
So nobody reads it.
The companies know this.
In fact, they bank on it.
Then there’s the language they use to write it. The class action filed
against Samsung in January 2026 alleges the company described its screen-sampling
as “processing” rather than saying it was collecting what you watch from every source.
But even switching off the tracking can be difficult.
According to The Markup, switching off tracking took 11 to 24 clicks on a Roku,
27 clicks on an LG, and anywhere from 10 to 37 clicks on a Samsung.
These settings were tucked inside submenus with arcane
names. None of which mean anything to a normal person holding a remote.
Consumer Reports asked actual TV owners to go find their privacy settings, and the results
were what you'd expect. As UCL Researcher Dr. Anna Maria Mandalari put it, “the average user
is unlikely to know what ACR is or that they can opt out” at all. Whereas, the “‘opt in’
is usually a single click during the initial setup… often buried in a wall of legal text.”
But the boldest move in the whole genre belongs to Roku.
In 2024, Roku pushed out new terms requiring users to give up their right to sue as part
of a class action. Users who declined found their televisions locked until
they consented. People who wanted to opt out of these enforced terms had
to physically mail a letter to corporate headquarters within 30 days of receipt.
Why would a streaming device company,
and television manufacturers in general, go through so much trouble?
Because the television was never the point.
The television business was supposed to be simple. A company builds a television,
sells it to you for more than it costs to make,
and pockets the difference. You then own the television and watch what you want to watch.
That’s the way commerce has worked since forever.
Vizio’s financial report from the fourth quarter of 2023 revealed that the hardware division,
the part that builds and sells televisions, lost $7.3 million dollars. The ad and data division,
which Vizio calls Platform+, made $105.4 million in gross profit in the
same 3 months. Across all of 2023, the television business lost $8.6
million while the ad platform cleared $364.9 million in gross profit.
In the shareholder letter, Vizio’s CEO, William Wang,
described the company as having “transformed… from a hardware company into a powerful CTV
platform company.” He wasn’t wrong. They lost money on virtually every TV they sold,
but made a fortune on what those televisions did afterward.
Across all of 2023, Platform+ brought in $598 million in revenue, with advertising
revenue up 36% in the final quarter alone. This had been the trajectory for years.
It’s the razor and blades model. Gillette sells you a cheap handle and profits on
the refills. Vizio sells you a cheap TV and profits on you.
At least the razor company tells you what the blades cost.
The payments start before you even get the tv home. In 2021, the Intercept reported that Google
pays TV manufacturers somewhere between $10 and $15 per unit just to have Google TV preinstalled.
The surveillance layer is a revenue stream for the manufacturer before the box leaves the warehouse.
LG plays the same game. Its advertising arm, LG Ad Solutions, pulled in roughly $700 million in
2024 and landed on the Inc. 5000 list of America’s fastest-growing private companies in 2025. Again,
the TV manufacturer is being celebrated for how fast its advertising business is growing.
The whole pot was worth an estimated $18.6 billion in smart TV ad spend in 2022.
And as televisions get more advanced, there’s no escape. So why not buy a dumb set?
Well, that’s becoming harder and harder.
Fewer than a half-dozen genuinely dumb models remain on the U.S. market, and they’re mostly
bottom-shelf panels from brands you’d struggle to name. Of course there’s demand, but TV
manufacturers know that a TV that can’t watch your back is a TV that only earns money once.
If you want the purest expression of what a television company is actually worth these
days, consider this: in 2024, Walmart actually bought Vizio.
A powerhouse retailer bought a TV manufacturer. Why? For
the advertising platform that came attached to millions of living rooms.
Each of those low-priced tv’s turned into virtual in-home billboards for Wal-Mart.
As one jaded Redditor commented after the deal,
“Now you can “unlock your Vizio 4k resolution with a monthly Walmart+ plan!”
For about a decade the television industry’s calculated gamble worked. Collect everything,
disclose it in a document nobody reads. If a regulator ever notices,
the fine will be miniscule.
Then Texas came in like a wrecking ball
The legal weapon they used was the Texas Deceptive Trade Practices Act, or DTPA.
Attorney General Ken Paxton used the same statute to hit Meta and
Google with billion dollar fines, so clearly he was onto something.
The DTPA allows penalties of up to $10,000 per violation,
with steeper penalties for violations affecting older consumers. The courts moved quickly.
On February 26th, 2026, Samsung agreed to stop collecting ACR data without consumer consent
and to put clear, conspicuous disclosure and consent screens on its TVs. 9 years after the
FTC nailed Vizio for the same behavior, a major manufacturer agreed to just ask permission first.
LG agreed to pop-up disclosures, website notices,
and a clear and simple way to opt-out. The settlement also included a provision
barring LG from transferring viewing data to the Chinese Communist Party.
But these are only Texas settlements which protect only Texans. If you’re TV in Ohio
or Oregon or Boston or Baltimore, the companies made no such promise to you.
They’re still harvesting every sound in your room and every pixel on the screen.
This is the reality of the smart television age. Privacy isn’t a universal right.
Even in the dark, your television is still watching you.
And if you're thinking the television is the only thing in your house spying on you,
we have bad news. Watch “Somebody Is Watching You Right Now” to find
out how you have no internet privacy. Or click on this.
